01.r: Adds the next step of the argument about Melchizedek.

02.r: The article, taken up by 'who receive' below: those of Levi's sons who receive the priesthood.

03.r: Opens the first side of a contrast; the other side, Melchizedek, follows with 'but' in the next verse.
03.n: Abbott-Smith says this particle usually looks ahead to a following δέ and is generally untranslatable. This study renders it 'on the one hand', as in Hebrews 7:8, so the reader can see the two sides of the argument.

04.r: Marks the group the priests are drawn from.

07.r: The son of Jacob from whom the priestly tribe descends.
07.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse under Levi the son of Jacob.

09.r: The office and work of a priest, which these men take up.
09.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'priesthood, office of priest' and lists only two New Testament uses, this verse among them. It is a different word from the one rendered 'priesthood' in Hebrews 7:11, ἱερωσύνη, so this study keeps it as 'priestly office'.

10.r: Present participle: those who receive the office, generation after generation.
10.n: The same verb, λαμβάνω, is used for receiving tenths in Hebrews 7:8. The BSB's 'who become priests' turns 'receive the priestly office' into one idea.

11.r: A charge laid on them by the law.
11.n: The Greek says they 'have a command'. The BSB turns this into 'the law commands'.

12.r: They hold the command as a standing duty.

13.r: To require a tenth from the people.
13.n: Abbott-Smith distinguishes the uses of this verb: with the thing as object, to pay a tenth of it; with a person as object, as here, to exact tithes from; he cites this verse for the second. The object is 'the people', so the priests are the ones taking. It is the compound of the verb rendered 'take a tenth' in Hebrews 7:6.

15.r: Israel, the people of God, from whom the tenth is taken.

16.r: The law is the standard and source of the command.

17.r: The law of Moses, already known to the reader.

21.r: The article with 'brothers'; English uses 'their' alone.
21.n: Greek says 'the brothers of them'. The article has no English of its own here.

22.r: Fellow members of the same nation, not only blood brothers.
22.n: Abbott-Smith records that in the Septuagint the word is used of a brother, of a neighbour, and of a member of the same nation. The last is the sense here: the people the priests tithe are their own kin.

24.r: Concedes a point that might have counted against the tithing.
24.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'although', used with a participle, and lists this verse.

25.r: The brothers, like the priests, are descended from Abraham.
25.n: A perfect participle in the accusative plural, agreeing with 'brothers': it is the people who are tithed who 'have come out of the loins of Abraham'. The perfect marks a descent that still defines them. The ASV's 'these' makes the reference clear.

26.r: Marks the source of their descent.

28.r: Abraham's body, as the source of his descendants.
28.n: The Greek is singular, 'the loin'; English idiom uses the plural. Abbott-Smith notes that the loin was regarded, as by the Hebrews, as the seat of generative power, and cites this verse.

29.r: The common ancestor of priests and people alike.
